facts.statement: The genus Megapaloelodus was once synonymized with the misspelled name Megapalaelodus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Megapalaelodus Wetmore 1951

facts.statement: American paleontologist Alden H. Miller named the genus Megapaloelodus in 1944 based on fossils found in South Dakota.
facts.quote: Megapaloelodus was named by American Alden H. Miller in 1944 on the basis of a fossil femur and tarsometatarsus collected from the lower Miocene Rosebud Formation of South Dakota.

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus fossils are primarily found in Miocene deposits across America, though the species M. goliath was discovered in Europe.
facts.quote: Megapaloelodus is primarily known from Miocene America, from South Dakota and Oregon in the north to Argentina in the south, but the species Megapaloelodus goliath was found in Europe.

facts.statement: An unnamed species of Megapaloelodus was discovered in Miocene sediments in Namibia.
facts.quote: Additionally, one unnamed species was discovered in Miocene sediments from Namibia.

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus species were typically larger than Palaelodus and likely lived in brackish lake environments.
facts.quote: Species of this genus are typically larger than those of Palaelodus and appear to have inhabited similar brackish lake environments.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Megapaloelodus may have been capable of locking its legs in a standing position.
facts.quote: Additionally, they may have been capable of "locking" their legs in a standing position.

facts.statement: Loye H. Miller described a fragment of a tibiotarsus and an ulna from late Miocene California and assigned it to M. connectens in 1950.
facts.quote: In 1950 Loye H. Miller described the fragment of a tibiotarsus and an ulna from the late Miocene of California, also referring it to M. connectens.

facts.statement: Pierce Brodkorb described the species M. opsigonus from Juntura, Oregon.
facts.quote: In addition to further finds from California, a second species was described from Juntura, Oregon by Pierce Brodkorb, M. opsigonus.

facts.statement: Jacques Cheneval transferred the species Palaelodus goliath to the genus Megapaloelodus in 1983.
facts.quote: In 1983 Jacques Cheneval published a major revision of the palaelodids of Saint-Gérand-le-Puy. Besides agreeing with prior studies that synonymized many of the European species, he also transferred Palaelodus goliath to the genus Megapaloelodus.

facts.statement: In 2002, Jiří Mlíkovský suggested that the genus Megapaloelodus should be synonymized with Palaelodus.
facts.quote: Czech paleontologist Jiří Mlíkovský disagreed with this assessment in 2002 and instead suggested that Megapaloelodus should be synonymized with Palaelodus.

facts.statement: Other authors consider the suggestion to synonymize Megapaloelodus with Palaelodus to be premature and criticize this taxonomic treatment.
facts.quote: However, this taxonomic treatment of the genus as a whole has been met with criticism and is considered premature by other authors.

facts.statement: The species M. peiranoi was described in 2009 from specimens found in Argentina.
facts.quote: In 2009 several specimens from Argentina previously only identified as an indetermined phoenicopterid were described as the species Megapaloelodus peiranoi.

facts.statement: The name Megapaloelodus combines the Greek word for 'great' with a misspelling of Palaelodus, meaning 'ancient inhabitant of marshes'.
facts.quote: The name Megapaloelodus combines the Ancient Greek word "mega" meaning "great" with a misspelling of the name Palaelodus, roughly translating to "ancient inhabitant of marshes", after the closely related genus primarily known from European deposits.

facts.statement: The name Megapaloelodus was chosen because the first discovered remains appeared larger than Palaelodus goliath.
facts.quote: The name was chosen to reflect the fact that the first discovered Megapaloelodus remains, belonging to M. connectens, appeared to have been larger than the already big Palaelodus goliath.

facts.statement: M. goliath is the earliest known species of Megapaloelodus, living from the Late Oligocene to the Middle Miocene, and is the only named species found outside the Americas.
facts.quote: M. goliath It is the earliest representative of Megapaloelodus, living from the Late Oligocene to the Middle Miocene, and is the only named species outside of the Americas.

facts.statement: The species M. opsigonus was found in the Pliocene Juntura Formation in Oregon.
facts.quote: M. opsigonus A later species, M. opsigonus, was found in the Pliocene Juntura Formation at Juntura, Oregon.

facts.statement: The species name M. opsigonus means 'born in a later age', referring to its appearance during the Pliocene.
facts.quote: The species name means "born in a later age" in reference to its appearance during the Pliocene.

facts.statement: The species M. peiranoi was discovered in the Late Miocene Andalhualá Formation of Argentina.
facts.quote: M. peiranoi The most recently described species, M. peiranoi was discovered in the strata of the Late Miocene Andalhualá Formation of Catamarca, Argentina.

facts.statement: Unlike Palaelodus and modern flamingos, the forearm of M. peiranoi was short and robust rather than elongated.
facts.quote: Unlike Palaelodus and modern flamingos, the forearm of M. peiranoi appears to have been short and robust rather than elongated.

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus differs from relatives by having a pronounced tubercle on the trochlea that articulates with carpal bones, located as a rounded point on the upper rim of the bone.
facts.quote: Megapaloelodus differs from its relatives through the pronounced tubercle located on the trochlea that articulates with the carpal bones, this tubercle is present as a rounded point that is located on the upper rim of the bone.

facts.statement: In Megapaloelodus, the tibiotarsus profile is indented by a deep, rounded notch accompanied by a large, hooked process.
facts.quote: In Megapaloelodus this is taken to an extreme, as the profile is not simply flattened but actually indented by a deep, rounded notch that is accompanied by a large, hooked process.

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus belongs to the family Palaelodidae, which connects modern flamingos and grebes.
facts.quote: Megapaloelodus is placed in the family Palaelodidae, a group of primarily Neogene stem-flamingos that are considered to be an important link between modern flamingos and grebes

facts.statement: Research indicates that the Palaelodidae family forms a sister group to the flamingo family Phoenicopteridae.
facts.quote: later research discovered that palaelodids instead formed a monophyletic sister group to phoenicopterids

facts.statement: The species M. peiranoi is hypothesized to be the most basal member of the genus Megapaloelodus.
facts.quote: Within the genus, M. peiranoi has been suggested to be its most basal member due to some similarities with basal mirandornithes like Juncitarsus

facts.statement: The genus Megapaloelodus was established by A. H. Miller in 1944.
facts.quote: genus_authority: A. H. Miller, 1944

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus lived from the Late Oligocene to the Early Pliocene.

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus likely had a less curved beak than modern flamingo species.

facts.statement: The validity of Megapaloelodus as a genus was argued by Brodkorb in 1961, Cheneval in 1983, and Baird & Rich.

facts.statement: A colleague suggested that notches on Megapaloelodus leg bones allowed the bird to lock its legs in an upright sleeping position.
facts.quote: a colleague suggested that this may have allowed these birds to "lock" their legs in an upright standing position while sleeping, thus stabilizing their resting posture

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus likely inhabited lakes that were sometimes highly saline or brackish.
facts.quote: It is possible that Megapaloelodus, much like many other phoenicopteriforms, inhabited lakes which at times may have been highly saline or brackish

facts.statement: M. goliath inhabited a brackish lake environment with cyclical wet and dry periods in Saint-Gérand-le-Puy, France.
facts.quote: In the French locality of Saint-Gérand-le-Puy, Megapaloelodus goliath is known to have inhabited a brackish lacustrine environment that underwent cyclical wet and dry periods

facts.statement: Megapaloelodus shared its habitat with the genera Palaelodus and Harrisonavis.
facts.quote: Here Megapaloelodus shared its environment with at least two other genera of flamingo. Palaelodus, which may be present in the form of several species, and the more derived flamingo Harrisonavis

facts.statement: Palaelodus is the only known palaelodid with preserved skull material, showing a straight bill unlike derived flamingos.
facts.quote: Currently, the only known palaelodid with preserved cranial material is Palaelodus itself, which shows a straight bill very different from that of derived flamingos
